# World Models {#ml-world-models .ml-prep}

Pause a recording just before the ego car enters the intersection. Ask for two futures from that same instant. In one, the ego car holds its speed. In the other, it brakes. A driving world model used for planning must represent some consequences of the proposed ego action. A visually persuasive continuation of the recording can give the same answer to both requests.

[Representations](#ml-world-representations) · [Latent dynamics](#ml-latent-dynamics) · [Action sensitivity](#ml-world-validation) · [SceneDiffuser](#ml-scenediffuser) · [Drive&Gen](#ml-drive-gen) · [City-scale simulation](#ml-citysim)

## Choose what the model will predict {#ml-world-representations}

| Representation | Example output | Question it can answer well | Information it may lose |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Agent states | Boxes, positions, headings and velocities | Which road users interact after ego brakes? | A missed object in the input tracker, glare or a sensor artifact |
| Occupancy | A grid giving the probability each cell is occupied at each time | Where might space become unavailable? | Agent identity and dependencies between occupied cells |
| Raw sensors | Future camera frames or lidar returns | How would a perception stack see this scene? | Physics can be wrong despite realistic texture |
| Learned latent state | A compact vector sufficient for a training objective | Which actions have high predicted return? | Small visual details that matter to a different task |

A **transition model** predicts \(p(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)\). An **observation model** predicts measurements \(p(o_t\mid s_t)\). A model of the other agents determines how they respond as the ego vehicle moves. These roles can share a neural network, but you need to know which variables can be changed independently in an experiment. A renderer conditioned on fixed future vehicle boxes can test camera perception under a new viewpoint. Studying whether other vehicles yield requires a mechanism that updates their boxes in response.

## Learn and roll out a latent state {#ml-latent-dynamics}

A **latent** is an internal variable the model infers. Start with an observation encoder that compresses a frame. A recurrent state-space model maintains a deterministic memory \(h_t\) of history and a stochastic latent \(z_t\). Given the previous memory, latent and action, compute \(h_t=f(h_{t-1},z_{t-1},a_{t-1})\). The **prior** \(p(z_t\mid h_t)\) predicts a distribution before seeing the new observation. During training a **posterior** \(q(z_t\mid h_t,o_t)\) uses the new frame as well. A decoder reconstructs the observation, and another head predicts reward from the state. [Hafner et al., PlaNet, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.04551)

One training objective minimizes reconstruction loss, reward prediction loss, and a weighted divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\). KL divergence is the posterior's expected log probability ratio \(\mathbb E_q[\log q-\log p]\). It vanishes for identical distributions. The reconstruction term encourages retention of observable detail. The KL term encourages a prior that can anticipate what the posterior learns when the frame arrives. Excessive compression may erase an occluded cyclist. A very informative posterior and a weak prior can produce excellent reconstructions and implausible imagined futures.

**Trace one step.** Suppose a latent event is “cyclist enters” and the observed history gives it probability 0.2. A frame revealing a wheel might update the posterior to 0.8. During training the decoder can use that wheel evidence. During an imagined rollout the future frame does not exist. Sample from the prior, take a candidate ego action, update memory and repeat. Feeding the logged future frame at every imagined step accidentally turns a multi-step test into a series of easier one-step predictions.

In **model predictive control**, roll out several action sequences in the latent space, evaluate predicted reward and choose the first action of a promising sequence. PlaNet uses a cross-entropy planning method that repeatedly samples candidate action sequences and refits a distribution to the best subset. In **Dreamer**, a policy and a value function learn from imagined trajectories so a trained actor can select an action directly. Both rely on the predictor in states induced by the planner. Test over an increasing imagination horizon and compare policy performance in an independent environment. [PlaNet, Algorithm 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.04551) · [Dreamer, §§3–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.01603)

## Test whether actions make the right difference {#ml-world-validation}

1. **Verify the data contract.** Align an action with the interval it affects. Check coordinate frames, units, control delay, and whether the action is a steering command, curvature, or future pose. In a straight segment, flipping left and right should mirror appropriate changes to the predicted ego path.
2. **Measure error versus horizon.** Evaluate one, two, four and eight seconds both with logged history refreshed at each step and in free rollout. Compare position and heading error, overlap and persistence of tracked identities. An error that grows sharply only in free rollout points toward accumulated state errors.
3. **Branch the same scene.** Apply a feasible brake command in one branch and maintain speed in the other. Share randomness where appropriate. Measure stopping distance and the following vehicle's reaction delay. Shuffle actions across clips as a control. If outputs barely change, past motion may dominate the action input.
4. **Check the consequence for decisions.** Freeze several planners with different levels of assertiveness. Compare their ordering in the candidate simulator with an independent, matched reference. Also compare absolute event rates, since every simulated score could have the same optimistic bias. Report uncertainty across scenes and inspect ranking reversals.

Only the executed action has a real recorded outcome at that instant. An observational association between braking and a pedestrian stepping out can arise because the driver already saw the pedestrian. To interpret an alternative action, specify hidden variables, how much action variation exists in comparable states, and the source of independent evidence. In controlled environments, randomized interventions can reveal both branches across repeated trials. In road logs, use matched scenarios and state what remains uncertain.

**Two kinds of uncertainty.** Some uncertainty comes from genuinely variable behavior given available observations. This is often called *aleatoric*. Limited knowledge about an unseen city or unusual vehicle adds *epistemic* uncertainty. An ensemble of models can reveal some disagreement about a new condition, while many samples from one model can describe different possible futures. Models trained on the same biased data can agree and still be wrong.

## SceneDiffuser · Keep a simulation responsive between decisions {#ml-scenediffuser}

Imagine predicting eight seconds of traffic just before the ego vehicle brakes unexpectedly. The first forecast may look plausible, but the vehicles behind now see a different situation. Jiang and colleagues (NeurIPS 2024) use diffusion to initialize a scene and update it as the simulation advances. They represent a scene as a table indexed by agent, time and feature, with entries such as position and heading. **Inpainting** means fixing known entries and generating the missing ones. Fix past states to forecast motion. Fix every existing agent and leave a row empty to generate an additional agent consistent with the scene. [Paper, Figure 2 and Section 3.1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/64ff8d0bf0b0fe2b872a42a0de9668f8-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=3)

### Two clocks in one simulation

Physical time advances as agents move. A diffusion step is a computation that refines a noisy future. Restarting sixteen denoising steps at every tick discards much of the previous prediction. **Amortized diffusion** keeps a rolling future, makes distant positions noisier than near ones, and refines that future as each new observation arrives. In Table 2, the medium model at 10 Hz used 96 evaluations for an eight-second rollout (16 for warm-up plus 80 updates), compared with 1,280 for full replanning. Its composite realism score rose from 0.492 to 0.673. One-shot generation scored 0.730 but could never respond to an external driver after initialization. The authors also supplied logged agent-validity masks and updated ego and traffic together, qualifications for comparisons with challenge entries. [Paper, Section 4.1 and Table 2](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/64ff8d0bf0b0fe2b872a42a0de9668f8-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=8)

**Interview question. Could a simulator match typical speeds while ignoring a braking lead car?** Yes. Matching the overall speed distribution leaves the relationship between lead-car braking and follower response unconstrained. In a proposed paired test, branch the same simulated scene into continued motion and gentle braking. Use shared random seeds, measure the follower's change in acceleration and response delay, and inspect minimum separation. Compare those responses with matched held-out braking events, while accounting for differences in traffic conditions.

## Drive&Gen · Test a camera simulator through a planner's decisions {#ml-drive-gen}

A generated intersection can look convincing and still place a crossing pedestrian too far from the vehicle. Wang and colleagues (IROS 2025) test whether the **same planner** behaves similarly on real and synthetic video for a matched scene. Their video diffusion model receives the ego vehicle's pose, road geometry, agents' 3D boxes, weather and lighting. Pose specifies position and orientation. This setup controls what the camera sees along a supplied trajectory. It leaves open the further question of how traffic would react to a newly chosen maneuver. [Paper, Sections III-A and III-B](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06209v1#S3)

### How the behavior permutation test works

Sample ten plans from the planner on the recorded clip and ten on the generated clip. For each plan, find its closest match in the opposite set, then average these distances in both directions. Pool the twenty plans, randomly split them ten-and-ten 1,000 times and recompute the distance. If the original real/synthetic split separates the plans more than almost all shuffled splits, the input source had a detectable effect on the planner. At a 5% rejection threshold, Table I reports that the test failed to detect a difference in 69.62% of scenes for the sun-angle-conditioned generator. Ten draws per group give the test limited power. A high fraction can also occur when a planner ignores a cue that matters. [Paper, Section III-A and Table I](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06209v1#S3.SS1)

### Which comparison isolates the value of synthetic training?

Table V holds fine-tuning steps constant. Training for 40,000 more steps on real clips gave a five-second average displacement error of 0.7469 on real validation data. Spending the first 20,000 steps on generated clips and the next 20,000 on real clips gave 0.7333. This experiment measures agreement with recorded trajectories. Testing closed-loop collision and progress outcomes would require executing the resulting policy in a reactive environment. [Paper, Section IV-C and Table V](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06209v1#S4.SS3)

**Interview question. How could two planners expose different errors in the same generator?** A planner that follows lanes may barely react to a missing pedestrian. A second planner sensitive to the crossing may change its braking point. Evaluate both on the same real/synthetic pairs. As a sensitivity check, deliberately shift a pedestrian box by a known amount, record each planner's braking response, and check the generated pedestrian's position independently. This separates a generator that ignored the instruction from a planner that ignored the pedestrian.

## SceneDiffuser++ and the population of a simulated city {#ml-citysim}

Imagine a 60-second trip built by repeatedly extending an eight-second forecast. A simulator that only advances the original agents eventually reaches streets that are empty, or keeps vehicles present long after they should leave the observed scene. Tan et al. (2025) model when participants appear and disappear as well as how they move. They also generate traffic-light states. In long rollouts many simulated cars have no unique counterpart in the log. The authors collect distributions of quantities such as new arrivals per window, vehicle speeds, and collisions. Jensen–Shannon divergence measures how differently two distributions allocate probability. Zero means identical distributions. [SceneDiffuser++, §§3–4](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.21976v1)

Hold the IDM planner fixed in Table 1. Replacing SceneDiffuser with SceneDiffuser++ reduces the 60-second composite divergence from 0.4797 to 0.2878, yet the collision-feature divergence rises from 0.3778 to 0.4361. This composite excludes the two signal metrics in that table. The new model better matches several aggregate properties of populated streets, while the collision statistic warrants separate investigation. As a follow-up, compare the timing and location of newly generated agents near the ego car, then repeat with a different planner. [SceneDiffuser++, Table 1 and metric definitions](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.21976v1#S4)
